rows.content:
A hash table is a data structure for storing key-value pairs, and its central promise is that looking up the value associated with a key usually does not require searching through every stored item. Instead, the table uses a hash function to turn a key into a number. That number is then reduced, often by taking it modulo the current number of buckets, so that it selects one bucket in an array. A bucket is simply a storage location in the table. Good hash functions are fast to compute, deterministic for the same key, and designed to spread different keys as evenly as possible across the available buckets. They do not need to produce a unique number for every key; indeed, different keys can easily land in the same bucket, and that situation is called a collision.

Collisions are handled by chaining. In a chained hash table, each bucket can hold more than one entry, typically as a small linked structure or sequence of key-value pairs. When a new key is inserted, the table computes its bucket and adds the entry to that bucket’s chain. When a lookup asks for the value belonging to a key, the table computes the same bucket index again and then examines the entries in that bucket one by one. For each entry in the chain, it compares the stored key with the requested key. If the keys match, the associated value is returned. If the chain ends without a match, the table can conclude that the key is absent. The equality comparison matters because reaching the right bucket does not prove that the key is present: a colliding key may share the bucket while being a different key altogether.

A small illustration makes this concrete. Suppose, purely for demonstration and not as a description of any real hash function, that cedar is assigned to bucket 2, maple is assigned to bucket 2, and pine is assigned to bucket 5. This made-up assignment deliberately creates a collision between cedar and maple. If cedar is inserted first and maple second, bucket 2 contains a chain with cedar followed by maple, while bucket 5 contains pine alone. To look up maple, the table computes the invented bucket assignment, arrives at bucket 2, and inspects its chain. It first compares cedar with maple and finds no match; then it compares maple with maple, finds the match, and returns maple’s stored value. To look up pine, it goes directly to bucket 5, where the first comparison succeeds. The example is not a real hash scheme; it simply shows how a bucket narrows the search and how a chain resolves the resulting collision.

The load factor is the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. It measures how crowded the table is. A low load factor means buckets are mostly short; a high load factor means chains tend to be longer and lookups may have to inspect more entries. To keep this under control, a hash table typically resizes when the load factor crosses a chosen threshold. Resizing usually means allocating a larger array of buckets, often roughly doubling the bucket count, and then reinserting every existing key according to the new bucket count. Reinsertion is necessary because the bucket index is computed relative to the number of buckets, so changing that number can move many keys to different buckets. The rehash costs time proportional to the number of entries, but it happens infrequently, so its cost is spread across many insertions; in amortized terms it does not dominate ordinary operations. After resizing, the load factor is lower, chains are shorter, and lookups become more reliably fast.

The expected lookup time is constant, or O(1) in asymptotic notation, under standard assumptions: the hash function distributes keys reasonably well, the table resizes to keep the load factor bounded, and the keys are not chosen adversarially to collide. In that setting, a lookup computes the hash, selects one bucket, and checks only a small average number of entries in that bucket. The number of comparisons does not grow with the total number of stored items, apart from the cost of hashing the key itself and occasional resize effects. The worst case is different. If many keys land in the same bucket—because of a poor hash function, an unlucky set of keys, or an adversary deliberately choosing keys that collide—then that bucket’s chain can contain nearly all entries. A lookup may then have to compare against almost every stored key, giving linear time, or O(n). Thus hash tables offer expected constant-time lookup rather than a guarantee of constant-time lookup in every possible case. The expected speed comes from good distribution and controlled load; the worst-case linear behavior comes from collisions concentrating entries into one long chain. That is how the lookup finds its way.
